description.en: The 45 degrees side bend uses a 45 degree hyperextension bench positioned sideways. The lifter hooks one foot in and bends sideways to load the top side obliques. It is a strong oblique builder.

en: Set up sideways in a 45 degree hyperextension bench.
Hook the bottom foot under the foot pad.
Place the top foot on the platform.
Cross the arms over the chest.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Lower the torso sideways toward the floor.
Pause briefly at the bottom.
Drive the obliques to lift the torso back up.
Targets the obliques
Strong side bend variation
Builds the core
Useful for core size
Trains the side abs

description.en: The band assisted floor glute ham raise is a Nordic style hamstring curl done on the floor with band assistance. The band is anchored overhead to support a portion of body weight during the lower. It builds the hamstrings.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead in front of you.
Place the band across the chest or under the arms.
Kneel on a soft mat with feet hooked under a sturdy support.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower the body forward toward the floor.
Use the band assistance to control the descent.
Engage the hamstrings to pull the body back up.
Continue for the working set.
Builds the hamstrings
Strong Nordic curl
Useful for beginners
Builds the glutes
Trains the posterior chain

description.en: The band bicep curl is the most basic at-home bicep exercise — stand on a resistance band and curl both ends up. The band provides increasing tension at the top of the curl, loading the peak bicep contraction more than the bottom. It is simple, effective, and portable.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Grip both ends of the band with palms facing forward (supinated grip).
Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides.
Curl both ends up toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows.
Squeeze your biceps at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds.
Keep your upper arms still throughout — only your forearms move.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Most basic at-home bicep exercise
Increasing tension at the peak contraction
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Joint-friendly
Simple execution

description.en: The band lying leg and hip raise adds band resistance to a classic leg raise with a hip lift at the top. The band increases tension in the lower abs and hip flexors.

en: Anchor a resistance band low on a sturdy point.
Lie on your back with the head away from the anchor.
Loop the band around the feet or ankles.
Brace the core and press the lower back to the floor.
Lift the legs up toward the ceiling against the band.
At the top, drive the hips up off the floor.
Lower the hips and legs back to the start with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Hammers the lower abs and hip flexors.
Band adds tension throughout the range.
Builds core strength with progressive resistance.
Carryover to hanging leg raises.
Easy to scale by adjusting band tension.
Develops anterior core stability.

description.en: The bar band standing single arm upright row uses one end of a banded barbell with one hand. The single arm upright row builds the side deltoids and upper traps while the bands add accommodating resistance.

en: Anchor a barbell in a landmine or load one end heavily as a counterweight.
Loop a band over the working end of the bar.
Stand tall with feet shoulder width apart.
Grip the bar end with one hand and let the bar hang at your hip.
Brace the core and keep the elbow soft.
Pull the bar up toward your chin by driving the elbow up.
Keep the elbow higher than the wrist throughout the pull.
Lower the bar slowly back to the start and complete all reps then switch.
Hits the side delts and upper traps unilaterally.
Bands accommodate the strength curve.
Single arm focus exposes imbalances.
Builds shoulder size and traps strength.
Joint friendly when performed with strict form.
Adds variety to two arm upright rows.

description.en: The bar close grip biceps curl is a barbell curl with the hands placed close together (about hip width). The narrow grip biases the long head of the biceps and adds forearm engagement compared to a standard grip. It is a strong arm builder.

en: Stand tall holding a barbell with both hands close together at hip width.
Set the elbows tight against the sides.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Curl the barbell up toward the chest by bending the elbows.
Keep the elbows fixed at the sides throughout.
Continue curling until the bar reaches the upper chest.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Strong bicep long head builder
Trains the forearms
Heavy load capacity
Builds bicep size
Useful arm builder
Strong barbell move

description.en: The barbell bench press is the most popular upper-body pressing exercise in strength training. Lying on a bench, you lower a loaded barbell to your chest and press it back up to lockout. It primarily develops the pectoralis major while heavily recruiting the front deltoids and triceps, and it serves as the benchmark for upper-body pressing strength.

en: Lie back on a flat bench with your eyes directly under the bar. Plant both feet firmly on the floor and create a slight natural arch in your lower back.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back, pinning them to the bench. Keep this tightness throughout every rep.
Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar (do not use a thumbless grip) and stack your wrists over your elbows.
Unrack the bar with straight arms and bring it over your chest. Take a deep breath into your belly and brace your core.
Lower the bar under control to the lower portion of your chest, allowing your elbows to flare to roughly 45 to 75 degrees from your torso, not pinned to your sides and not at 90 degrees.
Press the bar back up and slightly toward your face, finishing with your arms straight over your shoulders. Exhale at the top.
Repeat for the desired number of reps, then rack the bar safely with the help of a spotter when working near maximum loads.
Builds size and strength in the chest, front deltoids, and triceps
One of the most reliable measures of upper-body pressing strength
Allows progressive overload across a long career of training
Improves performance in sports requiring pushing power
Easily programmed across rep ranges for hypertrophy or maximum strength

description.en: The barbell elevated heel squat is performed with the heels raised on a wedge, plates, or weightlifting shoes. Elevating the heels allows for deeper knee flexion, more upright torso, and significantly more quad engagement than a flat-foot squat. It is a strong choice for quad-focused training.

en: Place small plates, a wedge, or wear weightlifting shoes to elevate your heels around 1 to 2 inches.
Set up under a barbell in a power rack with the bar across your upper back.
Step back with your feet shoulder-width apart, heels on the elevation.
Brace your core and pull the bar tight to your back.
Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees, allowing them to track over the toes.
Descend as deep as your mobility allows.
Drive through your heels to stand back up to lockout.
Maintain an upright torso throughout the lift.
Maximally targets the quadriceps
Allows deeper squat depth
Forces a more upright torso position
Useful for lifters with poor ankle mobility
Builds quad size and detail
Trains the same pattern as Olympic weightlifting shoe squats

description.en: The barbell lying tricep extension is essentially the same exercise as the barbell skull crusher / lying extension. You lie on a flat bench and lower a barbell toward your forehead by bending at the elbows, then extend back to lockout. It is one of the best mass-building tricep exercises.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a barbell or EZ bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Press the bar up to lockout above your chest.
Keep your upper arms vertical. Bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead.
Lower until the bar is just above your forehead.
Extend at the elbows to press back to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Keep elbows pointing up — do not flare them.
Use moderate weight and controlled tempo.
Heavy tricep loading for mass
Targets all three tricep heads
Allows progressive overload
One of the most effective tricep exercises
Builds lockout strength for bench press
Simple setup

description.en: The barbell standing calf raise places a barbell across the upper back and performs standing calf raises from a step or raised surface. It is essentially the same as the barbell standing leg calf raise — a free-weight alternative to the calf raise machine.

en: Set a barbell across your upper traps. Stand with the balls of your feet on a step or raised block.
Let your heels hang off the edge. Lower your heels for a full stretch.
Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top.
Lower under control. Full range every rep.
Use moderate weight.
Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Hold the rack or wall for balance if needed.
Free-weight calf loading
No machine needed
Full range of motion with a step
Easy to load progressively
Targets the gastrocnemius
Simple setup

description.en: The bicycle twisting crunch is the classic bicycle crunch that combines a torso crunch with alternating cycling leg motion and a twist. Each rep has you bringing the opposite elbow toward the opposite knee while extending the other leg. The dynamic pattern hits the rectus abdominis and obliques together.

en: Lie on your back with hands behind your head, elbows out wide.
Lift your shoulders off the floor and bring both knees up to 90 degrees.
Brace your abs hard.
Crunch up and twist to bring your right elbow toward your left knee.
At the same time, extend your right leg straight out.
Reverse the motion, twisting to bring the left elbow toward the right knee.
Extend the left leg as the right knee comes up.
Continue alternating in a smooth bicycle pedaling motion.
Hits abs and obliques together
Builds rotational core strength
No equipment required
Strong rectus abdominis activation
Trains hip flexors
Classic ab exercise

description.en: The bodyweight lying legs curl is performed lying on the floor with sliders or a folded towel under the feet on a smooth surface. The hips are bridged up and the heels drag in toward the glutes. The combination of hip extension and knee flexion challenges the hamstrings hard.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on a smooth surface.
Place sliders or a folded towel under each foot.
Brace your core and lift your hips off the floor into a glute bridge.
Maintain hip height throughout the rep.
Slowly extend your legs out by sliding the feet away.
Stop just before the hips drop.
Curl the heels back in toward your glutes.
Squeeze the hamstrings at the top.
Builds hamstring strength
Combines hip extension and knee flexion
No equipment beyond sliders
Useful for home training
Strong glute and hamstring builder
Improves posterior chain control

description.en: Butt kicks are a cardio warm-up drill where you run in place rapidly kicking your heels up toward your glutes. They activate the hamstrings, build cardiovascular conditioning, and improve running mechanics. They are a staple drill in track and field warm-ups.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms bent at 90 degrees, ready to pump.
Begin running in place by quickly kicking your right heel up toward your right glute.
As your right foot returns, kick your left heel up toward your left glute.
Continue alternating rapidly. Aim to bring your heels to your glutes (or as close as your flexibility allows).
Pump your arms in opposition to your legs.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly.
Keep your torso upright — do not lean forward.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set.
Activates the hamstrings dynamically
Excellent warm-up for running and lifting
Builds cardiovascular conditioning
Improves running mechanics
No equipment needed
Time-efficient warm-up drill

description.en: The butterfly yoga flaps are a dynamic seated hip opener performed by bringing the soles of the feet together and gently flapping the knees up and down like wings. This loosens the inner thighs, hip adductors, and groin. It is commonly used as a warm-up or cool-down for lower body training and yoga practice.

en: Sit on the floor with your back tall.
Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out to the sides.
Hold your feet or ankles with your hands.
Sit up tall through the spine.
Gently flap your knees up and down toward the floor.
Move at a comfortable rhythm without forcing range of motion.
Keep your spine long and your shoulders relaxed.
Continue for a comfortable duration.
Opens the hips and inner thighs
Improves hip mobility
Loosens tight adductors
Useful as a warm-up or cool-down
Calming and gentle on the body

description.en: The cable standing hip thrust is a unilateral glute exercise performed at a low cable pulley with an ankle strap on one leg. You hinge slightly forward, then drive the cabled leg back behind you using glute hip extension. The constant cable tension and standing position make it an excellent glute isolator without lying down.

en: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Strap it around your right ankle.
Face the cable machine. Hold the machine for balance.
Lift your right foot slightly off the floor. The cable should be under tension.
Hinge slightly forward at the hips for leverage.
Drive your right leg straight back behind you by squeezing your right glute. Keep the leg straight.
Continue extending until your right thigh is in line with or behind your torso. Squeeze hard at the top.
Slowly let the leg return forward under control.
Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides.
Direct glute isolation through hip extension
Constant cable tension throughout
Standing position requires no bench setup
Trains balance and core stability
Easy to load progressively
Targets one glute at a time

description.en: The calf raise from deficit with chair supported uses a small step or plate under the balls of the feet. The deficit allows the heels to drop below the step for a long stretch on the calves.

en: Place a small step or weight plate on the floor.
Stand on the step with the balls of the feet on the edge.
Hold a sturdy chair or wall for balance.
Brace the core and keep the legs straight.
Allow the heels to drop down below the step level.
Pause briefly at the bottom for a stretch.
Press up onto the toes by extending the ankles.
Squeeze the calves at the top and repeat.
Trains the calves through a long stretch.
Deficit position increases range of motion.
No equipment needed beyond a step and chair.
Carryover to running and sprinting.
Improves ankle mobility.
Develops calf size and strength.

description.en: The duck walk is a conditioning and mobility exercise where you walk forward while staying in a deep squat position. It builds tremendous quadricep endurance, hip mobility, and ankle flexibility. It is brutally challenging and is used in military training, wrestling, and martial arts.

en: Squat down into a deep bodyweight squat — as low as your flexibility allows.
Stay in the squat position. Do not stand up at any point during the walk.
Begin walking forward by taking small steps while maintaining the deep squat.
Keep your chest up as much as possible. Place your hands on your hips, in front, or behind your head.
Walk for the desired distance (10 to 30 feet) or time (15 to 30 seconds).
Turn around and walk back. Stay in the squat the entire time.
Your quads will burn intensely — this is normal and the point of the exercise.
Stand up only after completing the prescribed distance or time.
Builds extreme quadricep endurance
Improves hip and ankle mobility through loaded deep-squat position
Develops mental toughness
Excellent conditioning exercise
No equipment needed
Used in military, wrestling, and martial arts training

description.en: The dumbbell one arm y elevation raises a light dumbbell up and out at roughly 45 degrees from the body to form half of a Y position. The unilateral pattern targets the lower trapezius and posterior shoulder fibers that are often neglected. It is a key prehab move for healthy shoulders.

en: Stand or sit holding a light dumbbell in one hand.
Let the arm hang at your side with palm facing in.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Raise the dumbbell up and out at a 45 degree angle from your body.
Lift until the arm is roughly in line with your ear.
Keep a slight bend in the elbow throughout.
Pause briefly at the top and squeeze the lower trap.
Lower the dumbbell with control and complete reps before switching.
Targets the lower trapezius
Builds shoulder health
Useful prehab work
Improves posture
Single-arm focus
Light load is plenty

description.en: The dumbbell split squat is a loaded version of the bodyweight split squat where you hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. The added load builds serious single-leg quad and glute strength while exposing left-right imbalances that bilateral lifts can mask.

en: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Step into a split stance — right foot forward, left foot back.
Stand tall with chest up and core braced.
Lower your back (left) knee straight down toward the floor by bending both knees.
Descend until your back knee is just above the floor and your front thigh is parallel.
Drive through your front foot to stand back up. Keep torso upright throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps on the right side, then switch.
Keep the dumbbells at your sides — do not let them swing forward.
Increase load progressively as you get stronger.
Builds single-leg quad and glute strength with progressive load
Exposes left-right strength imbalances
Easier to load and balance than walking lunges
More accessible than Bulgarian split squats
Works at home with one pair of dumbbells
Trains grip as a secondary benefit

description.en: The jack knife on ball is a core exercise done in a plank with the feet on a stability ball. The lifter pulls the knees in toward the chest while rolling the ball forward. It is a strong ab and core builder.

en: Place the shins or feet on top of a stability ball.
Set up in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to feet.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Pull the knees forward toward the chest.
Roll the ball forward as the knees come in.
Pause briefly at the tucked position.
Extend the legs back to the start.
Loads the core
Strong ab builder
Trains stability
Builds the abs
Useful core move

description.en: The kettlebell lunge with twist combines a forward or reverse lunge with a torso rotation at the bottom position. You hold a KB at your chest and twist toward the front leg at the bottom of the lunge, engaging the obliques while building leg strength.

en: Stand holding a KB at your chest with both hands (goblet position).
Step forward into a lunge with your right foot.
Lower your left knee toward the floor.
At the bottom, rotate your torso to the right (toward the front leg).
Return to center, then drive through your front foot to stand.
Step forward with the left foot and twist to the left at the bottom.
Continue alternating.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Combines lunge with rotational core work
Builds oblique strength during lunging
Improves hip mobility and coordination
Engages the full body
Useful for sport-specific conditioning
Time-efficient compound exercise

description.en: The kettlebell seated one arm military press is a strict shoulder press performed seated with a kettlebell in one hand. The seated position eliminates leg drive and forces the shoulder to do all the work. The single kettlebell load also trains anti-lateral flexion in the trunk.

en: Sit on a bench with back support holding a kettlebell at the shoulder.
Keep the wrist neutral and the kettlebell resting on the back of the forearm.
Plant your feet flat and brace your core.
Press the kettlebell straight up overhead.
Lock out the elbow at the top with the kettlebell over your shoulder.
Resist any side lean from the load.
Lower the kettlebell back to the shoulder with control.
Complete reps before switching sides.
Builds strict shoulder strength
No leg drive cheating
Trains anti-lateral flexion
Single-arm focus
KB rack position is unique
Excellent shoulder builder

description.en: The kettlebell single arm sit up is a Turkish get-up style move where a kettlebell is held locked out overhead with one arm during a full sit-up. The combination challenges the core to work through a sit-up while the shoulder stabilizes the kettlebell overhead.

en: Lie flat on the floor with knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a kettlebell in one hand pressed straight overhead.
Lock the elbow and pin the bicep close to your ear.
Brace your core and keep the kettlebell stable.
Sit up while keeping the kettlebell locked overhead.
Reach a fully upright seated position with the arm still up.
Lower with control back to the floor while keeping the arm vertical.
Complete reps before switching arms.
Loaded core builder
Trains shoulder stability
Single-arm focus
Builds bracing skill
Useful Turkish get-up prep
Brutal full-body move

description.en: The knee touch crunch extends the hands toward the knees during a floor crunch. The reaching motion helps guide the crunch height and engages the abs through a consistent range. It is slightly easier than hands-behind-head crunches.

en: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Arms at your sides or resting on your thighs.
Crunch up, sliding your hands along your thighs toward your knees.
Continue until your fingers touch or pass your kneecaps.
Squeeze your abs at the top.
Lower under control.
The hand position guides consistent crunch height.
Slightly easier than hands-behind-head crunches.
Aim for 15 to 25 reps.
Guided crunch height through hand position
Slightly easier than hands-behind-head crunches
Beginner-friendly
No equipment needed
Builds ab contraction awareness
Simple and accessible

description.en: The kneeling plank tap shoulder is a regression of the standard shoulder tap plank. The lifter holds a plank from the knees and taps each opposite shoulder while keeping the hips level. The kneeling stance reduces the load and is great for beginners.

en: Begin in a high plank position from the knees.
Set the hands under the shoulders and the body in a straight line.
Brace your core and keep the hips level.
Lift one hand off the floor.
Tap the opposite shoulder with the hand.
Place the hand back on the floor.
Repeat with the other hand to tap the opposite shoulder.
Continue alternating shoulder taps.
Beginner friendly plank move
Trains anti-rotation core
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Useful core builder
Easy to scale

description.en: The landmine one arm bent over bench row is a unilateral row using a barbell anchored in a landmine. Bracing one hand on a bench supports the back while the working arm pulls the bar in a powerful row.

en: Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the working end with weight.
Stand to the side of the bar and place one hand on a flat bench.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the bench arm extended.
Grip the end of the bar with the free hand using a neutral grip.
Brace the core and keep the spine neutral.
Pull the bar up to your hip by driving the elbow back.
Squeeze the lat hard at the top of the row.
Lower the bar slowly back to full extension and repeat all reps then switch.
Builds unilateral back strength with the landmine arc.
Bench support reduces lower back load.
Hits the lats and rhomboids hard.
Constant load through the natural arc of the bar.
Develops grip and biceps strength.
Joint friendly for athletes with back issues.

description.en: The lying leg tuck hip back to right stretch is a supine glute and lower back stretch directed to the right side. Pulling one knee into the chest then guiding it to the right opens the lumbar spine and glute on that side.

en: Lie on the back with the legs extended.
Bend one knee and bring it toward the chest.
Wrap both hands around the shin or thigh.
Brace the core and keep the shoulders flat.
Pull the knee deep into the chest.
Guide the knee gently to the right side.
Feel the stretch through the glute and lower back.
Hold for the desired duration then switch sides.
Stretches the glute.
Decompresses the lower back.
Mobilizes the lumbar spine.
Useful for hip mobility.
Joint friendly stretch.

description.en: The lever banded chest press adds resistance bands to a plate-loaded chest press machine. The bands attach to the machine and the lifter, increasing resistance as the press extends. The accommodating resistance overloads the lockout and forces stronger pressing power, popular in strength training programs.

en: Set up a lever chest press machine with the desired weight loaded.
Anchor resistance bands to the base of the machine.
Loop the bands over the press handles or your wrists.
Sit on the seat with your back firmly against the pad.
Grip the handles at chest level with palms facing forward.
Brace your core.
Press the handles forward by extending your arms against both the weight and band tension.
Lower the handles back to the starting position with control.
Accommodating resistance through the press
Overloads the lockout
Builds pressing power
Different stimulus than standard machine press
Combines machine stability with band tension
Useful for strength specialization

description.en: The lever standing leg raise is performed on a hip flexion machine while standing upright. The pad rests against the front of the thigh as the leg lifts up against resistance. It is excellent for loading the hip flexors and lower abs in a functional standing position.

en: Stand on the lever leg raise machine with one foot on the platform.
Position the pad on the front of the working leg thigh.
Grip the handles for stability.
Stand tall with chest up.
Brace your core and keep your standing leg slightly bent.
Lift the working leg by driving the knee up against the pad.
Continue until the thigh is parallel to the floor or higher.
Lower slowly back to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Loads hip flexion
Builds hip flexor strength
Trains the lower abs
Functional standing position
Useful for runners
Improves hip drive

description.en: The medicine ball rotational throw is a power exercise where you stand sideways to a wall, hold a medicine ball, and explosively rotate to throw the ball into the wall using hip and core power. It builds explosive rotational strength critical for golf, tennis, baseball, and other rotational sports.

en: Stand sideways to a sturdy wall, about 3 feet away. Hold a medicine ball at your right hip.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees slightly into an athletic stance.
Rotate your torso to the right, loading the ball back behind your hip.
Drive through your right foot and explode by rotating your hips and torso to the left toward the wall.
Throw the ball into the wall with maximum force as you rotate.
Catch the ball off the bounce.
Reset and repeat. Complete reps on one side, then turn around and throw with the other side.
Aim for 6 to 10 throws per side. Maximum effort each rep.
Builds explosive rotational power
Develops oblique strength
Carries over to rotational sports (golf, tennis, baseball, MMA)
Excellent power-development exercise
Trains hip-to-shoulder force transfer
Time-efficient power training

description.en: The resistance band bent-over rear delt fly is a rear deltoid isolation exercise performed by bending over and pulling a resistance band apart in a fly motion. It targets the rear delts and mid-traps with constant tension from the band.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Grip both ends of the band. Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Let the band hang straight down with arms extended.
Raise both arms out to the sides in a fly motion until they are parallel to the floor.
Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Targets the rear delts with constant tension
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Useful for shoulder balance and posture
No bench needed
Builds mid-traps and rhomboids

description.en: The resistance band kneeling woodchop is a rotational core move performed kneeling with a band anchored high. The lifter pulls the band diagonally across the body from high to low. The kneeling position locks the lower body so the rotation comes from the core.

en: Anchor a resistance band high above shoulder height.
Kneel sideways to the anchor with the knee closer to the band on the floor.
Grab the band with both hands at the high side.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Pull the band diagonally across the body to the low far hip.
Rotate through the obliques as you chop.
Squeeze the core at the end range.
Return to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong rotational core builder
Trains the obliques
Stable kneeling base
Builds power transfer
Useful core move
Strong functional pattern

description.en: The reverse sliding leg curl on the floor with towel uses a small towel under the heels on a smooth floor. From a glute bridge, you slide the heels out away and pull them back in to train the hamstrings.

en: Place a small towel under each heel on a smooth floor.
Lie on your back with the knees bent and heels close to your hips.
Lift the hips into a glute bridge position.
Brace the core and keep the hips lifted.
Slide both heels out away from your body by extending the knees.
Stop just before the legs are straight.
Pull the heels back toward the hips by bending the knees.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Builds hamstring and glute strength.
Bridge position keeps the hips active throughout.
No equipment needed beyond a towel.
Excellent at home alternative to a leg curl machine.
Improves hamstring eccentric control.
Carryover to deadlifts and Nordic curls.

description.en: The side bridge with straight legs is a full side plank. With both legs extended and stacked, the long lever loads the obliques, glute medius, and lateral core hard.

en: Lie on your side with the legs extended and stacked.
Place the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder.
Stack the shoulders, hips, and feet in line.
Brace the core and squeeze the obliques.
Lift the hips off the floor by pressing the forearm down.
Form a straight line from the head to the feet.
Hold the position for the desired duration.
Lower the hips and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds full oblique and lateral core strength.
Trains the glute medius for hip stability.
No equipment needed.
Excellent foundation for advanced plank work.
Carryover to spine stability.
Develops anti lateral flexion strength.

description.en: The Smith machine decline bench press is a guided pressing exercise targeting the lower (sternal) head of the pectoralis major. The fixed bar path and safety hooks make it one of the safest ways to train the decline press to failure without a spotter.

en: Position a decline bench (15 to 30 degrees) inside a Smith machine so the bar tracks over your lower chest. Lock your feet under the leg pads.
Lie back with the bar above your lower chest. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Brace your core.
Twist the bar to unrack. Lower under control to your lower chest, elbows at 45 to 70 degrees.
Press back up to lockout, exhaling as you press.
Twist to re-rack on the final rep.
Set the safety stops just above chest contact for failure training.
The decline angle may allow heavier loading than flat or incline Smith pressing.
Targets the lower chest with guided safety
Allows training to failure without a spotter
Reduces anterior deltoid involvement vs flat pressing
Often allows heavier loading than flat pressing
Excellent for drop sets and high-rep work
Useful for lifters with shoulder issues on flat pressing

description.en: The standing hip flexor stretch is a practical stretch performed standing in a split stance, with the back foot elevated on a chair, bench, or wall behind you. By driving the hips forward and squeezing the back-leg glute, you stretch the hip flexor and rectus femoris of the back leg without needing to kneel.

en: Stand a few feet in front of a chair, bench, or sturdy surface.
Place the top of your right foot on the surface behind you. Your toes should point back, top of foot pressing into the surface.
Step your left foot forward to create a split stance. Bend your left knee slightly.
Stand tall and brace your core.
Squeeze your right glute hard. This tilts the pelvis posteriorly and intensifies the stretch.
Push your hips slightly forward while keeping the glute squeezed.
Feel the deep stretch in the front of your right hip and upper thigh.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Switch sides.
Stretches the hip flexors without kneeling
Practical for office or travel settings
Glute squeeze deepens the stretch effectively
Improves hip extension for better squats and running
No equipment needed (just an elevated surface)
Easy to integrate into daily routine

description.en: The strongman Hercules hold is a grip endurance event where you stand between two heavy pillars, posts, or handles and hold them at arm's length at your sides for maximum duration. The pillars try to pull your arms apart — you must resist. It tests elite grip and shoulder endurance.

en: Stand between two weighted pillars or cable handles set to heavy resistance.
Grip one in each hand at arm’s length at your sides.
Stand tall. Brace your core.
Hold the pillars in place. They want to pull your arms outward — resist.
Hold for as long as possible.
The event ends when you can no longer maintain grip or position.
Breathe steadily. Focus on squeezing.
Specialized strongman equipment required for competition version.
Tests elite grip endurance
Builds shoulder and arm endurance
Strongman competition event
Develops mental toughness
Simple concept, brutal execution
Builds anti-abduction arm strength

description.en: The suspender face pull is performed leaning back on a suspension trainer and pulling the handles toward the sides of the face. It targets the rear delts, rhomboids, and external rotators. It is excellent for shoulder health, posture, and upper back development.

en: Set the suspension trainer to about chest height.
Grab the handles with palms facing each other.
Lean back with arms extended in front of you.
Walk your feet forward to add lean for difficulty.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Pull the handles toward the sides of your face.
Lead with the elbows up and out to the sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Builds the rear delts
Improves posture
Strengthens external rotators
Useful for shoulder health
Builds upper back detail
No bench or cable needed

description.en: The suspender pull up uses suspension straps gripped above your head with the body hanging at an angle below the anchor. By pulling your body up toward the handles, you train the lats, biceps, and rear delts. The angled position is more forgiving than a standard pull up and easier to scale by adjusting body angle.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Sit or kneel below the anchor and grip the handles overhead.
Walk your feet under the anchor or extend them out in front.
Hang from the straps with arms fully extended.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Pull your body up by bending at the elbows and driving them down.
Continue pulling until your hands reach your shoulders.
Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Builds back without a pull-up bar
Easy to scale by changing body angle
Strong functional pulling pattern
Develops grip strength
Practical for home or travel training
Stepping stone to standard pull ups

description.en: The suspender wide grip inverted row is a TRX row done with the hands held wide. The wide grip flares the elbows and shifts focus to the upper back and rear delts. It is a useful TRX row variation for back width.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles wide with palms facing down.
Walk the feet forward until the body leans back.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the chest toward the handles with elbows flared.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Trains the upper back
Builds the rear delts
Strong wide grip row
Useful TRX move
Builds back width
Trains the biceps

description.en: The suspension trainer oblique rollout is a single-arm anti-rotation core move performed on TRX straps. The lifter grips one handle, kneels and rolls forward into an off-center extension. The asymmetric load forces the obliques to fight rotation and is a brutal core move.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip one handle with both hands together.
Kneel down facing the anchor.
Brace your core hard.
Slowly roll the body forward and to one side.
Continue extending until the body is at full reach off-center.
Hold briefly with the obliques braced.
Pull back to the start by squeezing the core.
Strong oblique builder
Trains anti-rotation core
Brutal asymmetric load
Strong TRX move
Useful core finisher
Builds rotational stability

description.en: The tuck-up is a dynamic core exercise where you start lying flat on your back, then explosively sit up while pulling your knees toward your chest, finishing in a tucked V-sit balanced on your sit bones. It builds dynamic core strength, hip-flexor power, and balance. It is a CrossFit and gymnastics staple.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs extended straight.
Brace your core. In one explosive motion, sit up while pulling your knees toward your chest.
Reach your hands forward to wrap around your shins or knees as you crunch up.
Finish balanced on your sit bones in a tucked V-sit position — knees pulled in, chest up.
Hold for one second.
Reverse the motion under control — extend your legs and arms back out, lowering to the start.
Do not let your hands or feet touch the floor between reps to maintain tension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Builds dynamic core strength and explosive power
Trains hip-flexor strength
Develops balance and body control
CrossFit and gymnastics benchmark
No equipment needed
Time-efficient core exercise

description.en: The weighted Russian twist is a loaded version of the Russian twist where you sit with knees bent, feet off the floor, and rotate your torso side to side while holding a weight. The added load drives oblique development beyond what bodyweight reps can achieve. It is a popular oblique-and-core exercise used for both strength and aesthetics.

en: Sit on the floor with knees bent at roughly 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor (or lifted off for more challenge).
Hold a weight plate, dumbbell, or medicine ball with both hands at chest height.
Lean back slightly so your torso is at roughly a 45-degree angle to the floor. Brace your core.
Lift your feet off the floor a few inches for added difficulty (or keep them planted for an easier version).
Rotate your torso to the right by twisting from the waist. Bring the weight to the right side of your body, just outside your hip.
Briefly tap the weight to the floor on the right side (optional) or pause briefly without touching down.
Reverse the motion and rotate to the left side, bringing the weight to your left hip.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of total reps. Rotate from the waist, not from the arms.
Builds the obliques with progressive overload
Trains rotational core strength
Develops anti-rotation and rotation control
Carries over to throwing, swinging, and rotational sports
Easy to scale by changing weight or foot position
Works at home with one weight plate or dumbbell
